story:
Mount Auburn Cemetery keeps a mapped inventory of its trees, and its biggest katsura comes out at 4.61 metres round. The cemetery's own plant inventory measured it again in September 2026 at 57.75 inches across the trunk and about 23 metres tall, the largest katsura anywhere in its records.

Massachusetts keeps a list of its biggest trees, and in 2022 the state measured a katsura in this cemetery at 177 inches round and 71.5 feet tall. The list gives no address beyond the cemetery's name. This tree comes within three percent of those figures, so it is very probably the same one, though neither record says so in as many words.

Katsura is planted for its autumn. In October the round leaves turn pink and yellow, and once they are down they give off a smell of burnt sugar that tends to reach you before the tree does. The cemetery opened in 1831, but nobody has put a date on this tree. The inventory gives no planting year. If you know when it went in, tell us.

It stands on the east side of the cemetery, in the section where Lime Avenue meets Fountain Avenue, close to Auburn Lake and about 40 metres from the great red oak of the same corner.

best_time.label: October, when the leaves turn pink and yellow and smell of burnt sugar once they fall

story:
This scarlet oak is older than the cemetery around it. When Mount Auburn opened in 1831, it was already growing here, and the cemetery's plant inventory still files it that way, as received in 1831 and of wild origin. Every lot, monument and avenue in this corner was laid out around a tree nobody planted.

How much older than 1831 it is, nobody knows. The record only says it was here first, which makes it at least 195 years old and possibly a good deal more. A visitor who logged it on iNaturalist in September 2026 described it the same way, as pre-dating the cemetery and therefore wild, and noted that cemetery staff had checked the identification.

The inventory puts the trunk at 51 inches across, about 4.07 metres round, and the height at 104 feet, close to 32 metres. Massachusetts lists a champion scarlet oak somewhere in Mount Auburn, measured in 2022 at 153 inches round and 88 feet tall. Whether that is this tree is not settled. A second big scarlet oak, by Mimosa and Heliotrope paths, is nearly the same size, and the state record names only the cemetery.

What is settled is that this one was standing before the first burial here, and that it has watched the whole of Mount Auburn grow up around it. It stands by Moss Path.

story:
Massachusetts lists its champion cedar of Lebanon in this cemetery and gives no more of an address than that. The state measured it in 2022 at 104 inches round and 68 feet tall, then wrote "Mount Auburn Cemetery" and left it at that.

The cemetery's own plant inventory narrows it down. Among its large trees there is one cedar of Lebanon, between Hazel Avenue and Indian Ridge Path, measured at 34.25 inches across the trunk, about 2.73 metres round, and 71 feet tall. Those figures sit within four percent of the state's, so this is almost certainly the champion. Neither record makes the match itself, so take it as a strong likelihood rather than a certainty.

The inventory names it as the subspecies stenocoma. It is an evergreen, which makes it one of the few trees on this hill that looks the same in January as in June, and a fair reason to come in winter, when the crowns around it are bare.

Nobody has dated it, and the inventory gives no planting year. If you know when it went in, tell us. About 30 metres away on Indian Ridge Path stands the cemetery's biggest Norway spruce, which makes a two-evergreen detour of it.

story:
Nikko fir grows wild in central Japan, and the biggest one Massachusetts has on record grows between two cemetery paths in Cambridge. The state recorded its champion in Mount Auburn in 2022 at 119.5 inches round and 75.5 feet tall, and the cemetery's own plant inventory has exactly one Nikko fir that fits.

That one stands between Pilgrim Path and Spruce Avenue. The inventory, last checked in October 2025, gives it a trunk 38.5 inches across, about 3.07 metres round, and a height of 77 feet, a shade over 23 metres. The two sets of figures agree within two percent. The state does not name the spot, so the pairing rests on species and size, which is as strong as this kind of match gets without a tag on the trunk.

Nikko fir is not a common sight outside Japan, and a champion of a rare species is a different thing from a champion oak. There may simply be few rivals. It is still a big conifer by any measure, and as an evergreen it looks much the same in every month you could visit.

Mount Auburn opened in 1831, and some 870 of the trees it has mapped since are 30 inches across or more. This is one of them. Nobody has published when it was planted. If you know, tell us.

story:
The champion zelkova of Massachusetts has a crown 93 feet across, wider than the state measured the tree to be tall. That was in 2022, when the register recorded a Japanese zelkova in Mount Auburn Cemetery at 166 inches round, 70.4 feet high and 93 feet from one side of the crown to the other. Japanese zelkova is the register's name for the saw-leaf zelkova.

The register gives no spot within the cemetery. The cemetery's own plant inventory points to this tree by Anemone Path and Mound Avenue, its largest zelkova, at 49 inches across and 84 feet tall. The trunk figures do not quite agree, about seven percent apart, and the inventory measured at two feet off the ground where the state measured at chest height, which accounts for some of it. So this is very likely the champion, and not proven to be.

What you can see for yourself is the spread. A crown nearly 28 metres wide throws a pool of summer shade over a good stretch of the lots beneath it. In autumn the leaves turn yellow to rusty orange, varying from tree to tree.

Nobody has dated it. The inventory gives no planting year, and the cemetery has been planting since 1831. If you know when this one went in, tell us.

story:
The dawn redwood on the Massachusetts big-tree list is not even the largest dawn redwood in Mount Auburn. The state measured one here in February 2022 at 156 inches round and 90 feet tall, and the cemetery's own plant inventory has a tree beside Willow Pond that matches it within one percent on girth and three on height. Over on Rosebay Avenue, though, the inventory has dawn redwoods bigger still, at 55.5 inches across against this one's 49.5, and none of them is on the state list.

So the champion is a champion of the register rather than of the ground, which says more about who got measured than about the trees. The pairing with this pond-side trunk rests on its size, since the state names only the cemetery.

It is a big tree all the same, about 3.95 metres round and 28 metres tall by the inventory's September 2026 figures. Dawn redwood is a deciduous conifer. It loses its soft needles every autumn, after they turn a reddish brown, which sets it apart from the pines and spruces around it for half the year.

Nobody has published when it was planted, which matters for a species science only described from living trees in the 1940s. An early date would make it one of the first in the country. If you know the story, tell us. About 25 metres away, by Sedum Path, stands the cemetery's tall Himalayan pine.

story:
This pine stands 101 feet tall, close to 31 metres, and its species comes from the Himalaya. The cemetery's own plant inventory measured it in September 2026, with a trunk 32.75 inches across, about 2.61 metres round, which is slender for that height. It is built upward rather than outward.

Massachusetts lists its champion Himalayan pine in Mount Auburn, measured in 2022 at 96 inches round and 91.1 feet tall. The state gives no position inside the cemetery, and this is the only Himalayan pine of any size in the inventory, so it is almost certainly the same tree. The figures sit about seven percent apart, and the state's height is ten feet lower, so read the champion title as very likely rather than certain.

It keeps its needles all year, so the tree you see in February is the tree you see in July. Its neighbour 25 metres away by Willow Pond is a dawn redwood, a conifer that does the opposite and stands bare from November.

Nobody has published a planting date for it, and the inventory gives none. If you know when it went in, tell us.

story:
The next biggest Norway spruce in Mount Auburn's plant inventory is 36.5 inches across. This one is 56. That gap is wide enough that the cemetery's record and the state's both point at it, even though neither says so outright.

Massachusetts lists a champion Norway spruce in the cemetery, measured in February 2022 at 194 inches round and 69.5 feet tall, with no position given. The inventory's figure for this tree on Indian Ridge Path is 177 inches round, taken just six inches above the ground, across the flare of the roots, and a height of 65 feet. A measurement that low flatters any trunk, so the comparison with the other spruces is not quite like for like. Even so, nothing else in the cemetery comes close, and the champion is very probably this tree.

Norway spruce is a European tree, a long way from home in a Cambridge cemetery. It is evergreen, so it looks the same in every season, and with the cedar of Lebanon about 30 metres away it makes a short winter walk of two conifers.

The inventory gives no planting year and nobody has published one. The cemetery has been planting since 1831, which bounds the question without answering it. If you know when this spruce went in, tell us.

story:
Mount Auburn's plant inventory gives this red oak a trunk 68 inches across, a figure so large it may take in a second stem. Even allowing for that, it is the biggest red oak the cemetery has on record, about 31 metres tall, and it was here before the cemetery was.

The inventory files it as received in 1831 and of wild origin, which is its way of saying the tree was already growing when Mount Auburn opened that year. That makes it at least 195 years old, with no record of how much older. It stands in the section where Lime and Fountain avenues meet, and everything around it, every lot and every monument, came later.

What it does not have is a state title. Massachusetts lists several Mount Auburn trees as champions, but no red oak among the cemetery's rows, so the only measurements here are the cemetery's own, last checked in August 2026 and measured that September. The 5.7-foot diameter is worth taking with some caution for the reason above. The height, 103 feet, needs no such hedge.

It is one of two big oaks the inventory records as older than the cemetery. The other is the scarlet oak by Moss Path, taller and slimmer. This one is the heavyweight. About 40 metres away in the same section stands the cemetery's biggest katsura.

story:
Massachusetts gives directions to its second-largest London plane in five words, one of them misspelled. The register line reads "Accross from 40 York St", in Wellington-Harrington, and nobody has published a better address.

The tree behind that line is 480 centimetres round, 79 feet tall and 79.5 feet across the crown, so it is very nearly as wide as it is high, about 24 metres both ways. The state measured it in August 2025. Only one London plane in the state is bigger.

It is a street tree, not a park tree. There is no fence, no lawn and no visitor path, just a residential block in east Cambridge and a crown that spreads over it.

Our pin sits on the building at number 40, because that is what can be placed. The tree is across the road from it, perhaps 20 metres off. Look for the crown, which at that width should be hard to miss on a residential street.

Nobody has dated it, and the register gives no planting year. If you live on York Street and know its history, tell us.
